name: Sovereignty (Sovranty, Lady of Sovereignty, Flaith)

sources: Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 10.

O’Brien, Marie Cruise. “The Female Principle in Gaelic Poetry.” In Woman in Irish Legend, Life and Literature, edited by S. F. Gallagher, 26–37. Irish Literary Studies 14. Gerrards Cross, Bucks: Colin Smythe, 1983.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Sovereignty, also called Sovranty or the Lady of Sovereignty or Flaith, is the goddess of the land. In sacred Ireland she was seen as the bride of the king, wedded to him at his inauguration. Her form varies in the tales. She may be the unnamed loathy hag who offers Niall a drink at her sweetwater well and then asks a kiss in return. She may be Ériu, the titular goddess of the island, or fierce and willful Medb, who weds one king after another. Yet the thought beneath each mask is one. The king's duty is to keep the land fertile by righteous rule, to give welcome to all, and to honor the sacred vows and taboos that bind his office. Should he fail, his reign is lost. So it was with Conairee, who broke his vows and died a horrible death.
